extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, designers, and craftsmen interested in principles of ornament, proportion, and architectural design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines for using ornament, proportion, and abstraction in architectural design: where ornament belongs, what counts as architectural ornament, and key proportional rules and anti-patterns. Emphasises appropriateness of form, hierarchy, and restraint rather than formulaic copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be appropriate to the architectural style and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament that belongs to one context (e.g., garlands on a head) is useless or offensive when transplanted to an incompatible building or surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: carved garlands hung upon a wall look withered and useless; if a circular ornament is wanted, use a flat circle of colored marble or a solid ring instead (Casa Doria example). Do not force decorative motifs into places where their original meaning or function is lost ('Why not also carve pegs, and hats upon them?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid isolated, fragmentary applied ornaments unconnected to structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attach excrescences or isolated decorative pieces that are unharmonious with the building's lines or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: dripstone shaped like a drawer-handle over square-headed windows — 'a monster' that looks glued on, has harsh broken lines, no architectural support, and no harmony with structure or decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not decorate objects of active, occupied, or practical use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where people are at work or in a state of business (no repose), ornament is inappropriate and becomes valueless or offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General law: 'Wherever you can rest, there decorate; where rest is forbidden, so is beauty.' Anti-examples: shop counters, millstones, tools, railroad stations. Such decoration satiates the eye, vulgarises forms, and associates fine motifs with vulgar uses (Greek mouldings over grocers' shops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Places of repose are the right locations for beauty and ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament belongs where the mind can calmly receive and appreciate it—places and moments of pause and repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good street ornament: fountains where people pause (pitcher resting, moment of refreshment), gondolas in Venice (no couch of rest like the gondola). The degree and nature of external or internal decoration depends on conditions of probable repose and local circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not cloak or disguise necessary functions with inappropriate decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using beautiful forms as masks that conceal or gloss over functional necessities, since this both fails the function and degrades the ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: decorative 'roses' used to conceal ventilators on chapel roofs—these borrow fine designs but are invisible in place and afterward dishonor the form; the congregation gains no pleasure and prototypes are deprived of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament should be imitative of natural forms, ranked by nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament ought to imitate or suggest natural existences; forms representing higher orders are nobler (human form > animals > flowers > stones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich ornament combines many orders (rock, fountain, river, herb, fruit-tree, creeping thing, bird, beast, man, angel); the architect can only represent certain severe characters of form, those which require intellectual examination to appreciate (the 'written or sealed impression' of a thing sought out).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two essential marks of architectural treatment: Proportion and Abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture requires a prominent sense of proportion and a disciplined abstraction of imitated forms; these distinguish architectural ornament from pictorial or purely sculptural work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike landscape painting (which may sacrifice proportion to character) or sculpture (which can be more pictorial), architecture 'delights in Abstraction and fears to complete her forms.' Proportion and abstraction determine how ornament is chosen and treated architecturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion rule: have one principal (supreme) thing in a composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever proportion exists, one member must be larger or otherwise supreme over the rest; composition requires unequal elements bound together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kept as a simple rule: 'Have one large thing and several smaller things, or one principal thing and several inferior things, and bind them well together.' Anti-examples: pinnacles without a spire, towers that overpower the central mass (unless intentionally made unequal), buildings like King's College Chapel which look like 'tables upside down' due to lack of a dominant centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry relates to horizontal division; proportion to vertical division — avoid equal vertical divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry is appropriate for horizontal divisions (halves, thirds), but vertical equality (cutting a spire or tower into equal vertical parts) is generally wrong and creates ugliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cutting columns in half with projecting architraves or dividing spires by bands halfway up. Preferred solutions: two bands and three parts in spires (Salisbury), regular increase or decrease of division heights (Doge's Palace), or alternating proportions in tower body, belfry, and crown (St. Mark's campanile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion requires at least three terms (three-part relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proportional composition needs three or more parts to achieve proper relation; two equal parts give only symmetry, not composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural practice: three vertical parts are about best in elevation, five in horizontal extent, with possible freedom to five or seven in details but not more without confusion. Example: pinnacles + spire + tower form three terms; botanical proportions (Alisma) illustrate subtle diminishing relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and relative sizing in mouldings and tracery
rubrics_metrics.description: In mouldings and tracery, members must be arranged in orders with one clearly larger and others progressively subordinate to create a harmonious whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Rouen cathedral: a tracery of four divisions where the leaf moulding is largest, outer roll next, then intermediate and innermost rolls; capitals and shafts scaled so smaller members have smaller capitals and are lifted to align visually. Such detailed alternation avoids heavy awkwardness in central groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to teach proportion by fixed mathematical formulas; cultivate eye and intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions are too varied and unique to be prescribed by set numeric recipes; teaching should prevent gross mistakes with a few general laws rather than provide fixed ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Teaching proportions by copying measured parts of fine works is as futile as teaching melody by giving mathematical relations of certain pieces. Useful preventive laws include the supremacy rule, three-term rule, and avoidance of equal vertical division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction: represent only those aspects of a form necessary for architectural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: When sculpture or carving is used as architectural ornament, it should abstract and include only the characteristics necessary for its place and effect, rather than attempting full naturalistic completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the architecture frames the sculpture or the sculpture ornaments the architecture; if the latter, the sculpture's first office is not to represent fully but to 'gather out of them those arrangements of form which shall be pleasing to the eye in their intended places.' The degree of completeness depends on place and circumstance—pure abstraction can be severe and wearisome, so balance is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of abstraction/completeness must suit place and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: How far ornament is worked toward completeness (naturalistic finish) depends upon its place, its association, and other circumstances; neither pure abstraction nor absolute completion is universally right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some purely abstract styles (early English) offer severity that may tire the eye after long exposure; other more completed treatments (Rouen moulding vs Salisbury dog-tooth) may be nobler in certain contexts. Architects must judge per case rather than apply blanket mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using ornament that reduces the appreciation of original exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheap or vulgar repetition of fine forms in inappropriate contexts diminishes public appreciation of the prototypes from which they are copied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When beautiful forms are constantly used on vulgar buildings or in unconscious places (e.g., Greek cornices on cheap shopfronts), people become satiated or desensitised and derive less pleasure from authentic works (e.g., prototypes in museums or churches).
